« On touche à l’histoire. On ne peut pas: “We’re touching history. We can’t rewrite it; we continue it, we write ourselves into it and we change it.”
Le 21 juin marque la Journée nationale d: June 21 marks National Indigenous Peoples Day. On that day, we celebrate the nations that have lived on unceded territories for millennia. After the death of George Floyd under the knee of a police officer in Minneapolis last month, people around the world took to the streets to protest racism and police brutality, as well as the racist and colonialist foundations of our societies and what publicly represents them: certain statues and monuments. Last Tuesday in Montréal, the statue of Christopher Columbus in Parc de Turin was vandalized. It was covered in red paint and “BLM” graffiti (for Black Lives Matter).
Le dimanche précédent, sur le boulevard: The previous Sunday, on René-Lévesque Boulevard in Montréal, the statue of John A. Macdonald had once again been splashed with purple paint and vandalized. Among other things, it bore the following message: “The RCMP rapes Indigenous women and kills Indigenous men.”
En ce moment circule une pétition demand: A petition is currently circulating asking the City of Montréal to take down this statue. It has already been signed by 16,000 people. A similar petition targets the statue of James McGill, a slave owner, in Montréal. Craig Commanda, an Indigenous student and artist from the Kitigan Zibi community, explains that John A. Macdonald, who was Canada’s very first prime minister, is “the architect of the RCMP, of the residential schools and of the racist legislature that imposed the railway on the Canadian West.”
Il estime qu’une statue de ce personnage: He believes that a statue of this figure is a glorification of white supremacy. “Taking it down would bring down his ideas and make room for a better world,” he says. According to historian Aly Ndiaye, also known as Webster, Quebec’s history is marked by the enslavement of 4,185 people, three-quarters of whom were Indigenous. He says most streets in Quebec are named after people who advanced the colonial project. Last week, Robert Jago, a Montréal-based columnist and member of the Kwantlen Nation, said he was “worried” about the “well-being” of the Columbus statue in Montréal. “With all these people tearing down Columbus statues, I hope the one in Parc de Turin is OK. It’s right there if you want to make sure it’s safe,” he wrote ironically on his social media. “People who want to leave these statues on their pedestals argue that the accomplishments of the figures they represent outweigh their crimes and that those crimes are essential to human history. I’m certain that future generations will associate Columbus’s name only with the crimes tied to his legacy,” he says in an interview.
Quand on lui demande par quoi, selon lui: Asked what should replace the statues of Macdonald and Columbus, Mr. Jago answers that Canada was built by three nations – the English, the French and the Indigenous peoples – and that he would like that reality to be reflected in public space. He thinks, however, that we live in an era when bronze statues no longer carry the weight of history the way they once did, and that it’s time to move on. According to Ellen Gabriel, a Kanienkehaka from the Kanesatake community, we should look at the importance we give to human statues. “It’s time to think beyond human existence and truly consider the importance of the natural world,” she says, reflecting on how Kanienkehaka history is represented. And if these statues stay on their pedestals, is it enough to add a plaque beneath them with explanatory text? That is what Cindy Blackstock, executive director of the First Nations Child and Family Caring Society of Canada, did. The McGill social work professor worked with Beechwood Cemetery in Ottawa in 2017 on the monument to Nicholas Flood Davin, adding a plaque noting his role in implementing the residential school system, which caused the suffering of several generations of Indigenous people and the deaths of 4,200 children.
Jaime Morse, Nehiyaw/Michif et fondatric: Jaime Morse, Nehiyaw/Michif and founder of Indigenous Walks in Ottawa, spends a lot of time analyzing statues and monuments and telling their stories as part of her cultural work. She first thought the statues should stay in place with a plaque added, but today she believes these figures are already part of history.
« Les statues sont sur des piédestaux, c: “Statues sit on pedestals; they’re symbols of who runs the city. We don’t need them. They can represent oppression and are an imposition of the ruling power. A young person doesn’t really see themselves in them and may even internalize a sense of inferiority from being around them. There are no real signs in them that we are on unceded Anishinabe territory. We need more opportunities to tell other stories in particular places,” she says. According to Guy Sioui Durand, a Wendat sociologist and art critic from the Wendake community in Quebec, colonial statues are reminders of society’s deep memory. “We’re touching history. We can’t rewrite it; we continue it, we write ourselves into it and we change it.”
Il estime que, si on devait faire tomber: He believes that if the Macdonald statue were to come down, it should be placed in a museum of toppled statues. Leena Minifie, a Gitxaala producer-researcher on a documentary series, explains that Indigenous history is simply not recognized at present. “These are tiny representations, chosen to glorify white people. We need to recognize those who contributed to the enormous changes this country has gone through, those who sacrificed themselves and were ignored by Great Britain.
It’s time to set things right.” In Ottawa, Canada’s capital, a few statues honour the place of Indigenous peoples in Canadian history. They notably depict figures who played an important role in securing trade or peace – including Joseph Brant, Tessouat and the nameless Anishinabe scout – not to mention the National Aboriginal Veterans Monument.
Au Canada, il y a plus de 690 statues de: In Canada, there are more than 690 statues of historical figures, but according to the website <l1>heroines.ca</l1>, only 20 depict women, and of those, barely four are dedicated to Indigenous women: the Spirit of the Beothuk in Newfoundland, Kateri Tekakwitha at the Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré Basilica near Quebec City, Shannen Koostachin in New Liskeard, Ontario, and the statue dedicated to missing and murdered women and girls near the police station in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, inspired by the story of Amber Redman, who disappeared in 2005.
